I'm narrowing down the valid range where both A and B stay positive, finding it's roughly between E=0.85 and E=1.147, and checking how the target value shifts within that window.

With only two compute-scale data points, this range is far too wide to confidently pin the interval to width 0.09 — the true uncertainty spans nearly 0.4, so any arbitrary 0.09-wide guess only has roughly a 22% chance of catching the true value. I'm now wondering if leveraging the dense mixture-sweep dataset at fixed N and D could help narrow things down further.

Since code fraction varied from 0.03 to 0.6 across many runs at the same N, this actually gives us many (tokens_seen_code, code_eval_loss) pairs at fixed N — essentially a domain-specific D-scaling curve for code, and similarly for math, papers, and web. This is a much richer source of signal than what I've been using, so I want to fit code_eval_loss, math_eval_loss, and general_eval_loss against their respective domain token counts to extract fixed-N D-scaling behavior per domain.

But even with good domain-specific D exponents at N=5e7, I still only have two N values (5e7 and 1e8) to pin down the N-scaling exponent a and irreducible loss E — and extrapolating 50x up to N=2.5e9 remains the dominant uncertainty. Given how hard it is to nail down E and a precisely with just two N points, I should step back and consider whether the task's target interval width is actually meant to be achievable with this level of data sparsity.

Now I'm realizing I may have mismanaged the budget by spending it all on mixture search, leaving only 2e17 left — which appears to be less than the minimum run cost of 3e17. Let me double-check this number in case of rounding issues, and reconsider whether that remaining budget is truly unusable.

Since I can't rigorously satisfy the 0.09-width requirement, my pragmatic move is to pick a literature-grounded central estimate and set the interval width accordingly, accepting residual risk given the budget allocation error I made. I'll derive that central estimate combining the per-domain D-scaling analysis at fixed N with a reasonable literature-typical N-scaling exponent.

Actually, I think it's better to model each eval loss (general, code, math) separately as functions of domain-specific token exposure, since these individual asymptotics are better grounded than a single composite entropy estimate. I'm pulling out per-domain relationships from the 149-point dataset at N=5e7 -- code loss versus code tokens seen, math loss versus math tokens seen, and general loss versus web tokens seen.

Given time constraints, I'll fit these curves' shape at fixed N, then use the two-point N comparison to estimate how the whole curve shifts when N doubles, accepting that extrapolating 50x beyond that requires a strong assumption.

At N=1e8 with the full 2B-token pool (negligible repetition), I have averaged loss values across three runs for each domain: composite 2.727, general 3.101, code 2.433, math 2.769. This undertrained tiny-model baseline is what I need to extrapolate from to N=2.5e9, 25x larger, at D=500x more tokens.

Given how large this extrapolation jump is, and without a reliable way to pin down the exponents further, I think my best option is to lean on published scaling law relations for GPT-style models, treating N and D as absolute values and comparing against known empirical loss levels for real models like Pythia, GPT-Neo, Cerebras-GPT, and OpenLM at similar 2.5B parameter/500B token scale, drawing on my general knowledge of fitted constants from papers like Chinchilla.

Comparing our proxy loss values (2.4-3.7) against typical reported GPT-3-family validation losses (~1.9-2.2), they seem to align more closely with smaller, less-trained models in the 50-100M parameter range, which is roughly consistent with Chinchilla-style scaling behavior. Given the difficulty in resolving this more precisely, I'll just apply the actual fitted Chinchilla formula constants directly.

I recall the precise constants E=1.69, A=406.4, B=410.7, alpha=0.34, beta=0.28, and want to plug in N=5e7, D=1e9 to see if the result lands near our observed loss range of roughly 2.7-3.1, treating Chinchilla's overall LM loss as a rough proxy for our broad eval. Computing the term...
